analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to set enforceable national drinking water limits for PFOA, PFOS, 1,4-dioxane, and perchlorate.
analysis.headline: The bill was never voted on; it sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee until the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Safe Drinking Water Act to force the EPA, within two years, to set enforceable national limits on four contaminants: PFOA and PFOS (the "forever chemicals" linked to cancer and other health problems), 1,4-dioxane, and perchlorate. It was introduced by Senator Gillibrand with Senator Schumer and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up. It died at the end of the 115th Congress without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly six million or more Americans whose water has been contaminated with PFAS, plus residents served by systems with 1,4-dioxane or perchlorate. Communities near military bases, airports, and industrial sites — the main PFAS sources — had the most to gain, because enforceable federal limits would have required utilities to test and treat water and created legal accountability for polluters.

how_it_helps.text: It sets a hard two-year deadline for EPA to issue enforceable national drinking water limits for PFOA and PFOS, the chemicals behind the Hoosick Falls, NY contamination crisis in the sponsor's state.
It also requires national limits for 1,4-dioxane and perchlorate, two other contaminants without enforceable standards.
Because the requirements are statutory, EPA cannot simply decline or delay the rulemaking the way it can with discretionary regulatory agendas.

analysis.who_pays: Water utilities and their ratepayers would fund testing and treatment; chemical manufacturers, industrial dischargers, and firefighting-foam users like the military would face compliance and liability costs.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall on public water systems, and ultimately on ratepayers, particularly in communities whose water requires expensive treatment for PFAS, 1,4-dioxane, or perchlorate.

The two-year deadline for nationwide standards was aggressive; the underlying health and treatment science for PFAS was still developing, and a rigid statutory deadline could force standards before key questions were settled.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real, documented gap: PFOA and PFOS were unregulated in drinking water despite links to cancer and other health harms, and millions of Americans drank contaminated water. Costs fall on water systems and their ratepayers to install treatment, and on dischargers like chemical makers and military/firefighting sources. The main design weakness is that it left standard-setting details to EPA rather than setting numeric limits, but the core benefit — enforceable national limits on a toxic family of chemicals — was substantial and never enacted.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 2, 2017 and read twice, then referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works — the only action ever taken on it.
No further actions appear in the record: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no House companion action.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill died in committee without receiving a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers and other PFAS polluters benefited from continued delay, since no enforceable federal drinking water limits for PFOA and PFOS were created during this Congress.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require EPA drinking water standards for PFOA, PFOS, 1,4-dioxane, and perchlorate.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to committee on the day it was introduced and never reported it out or held a markup.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill got no action in the Republican-led committee; no roll-call votes were ever taken.

industries.note: Enforceable drinking water limits would raise liability and cleanup exposure for companies responsible for perfluorinated pollution.
Utilities in contaminated areas would bear testing and treatment costs, some passed to ratepayers.
New national standards create demand for filtration technology and contaminant testing.

industries.industry: Department of Defense and firefighting-foam users
industries.note: Military bases and airports are major PFAS sources from firefighting foam; enforceable water limits raise their remediation obligations.
